issue.title: Bitcoin Kernel Library Project Tracking
issue.body:
#### Project Board for pull requests past and present: https://github.com/orgs/bitcoin/projects/3

This is the tracking issue for the bitcoin kernel library (`libbitcoinkernel`) project.

The bitcoin kernel project extracts Bitcoin Core's consensus engine. The kernel part of the name highlights one of the key functional differences from the deprecated libbitcoinconsensus and in fact, most libraries: it is a stateful library that can spawn threads, do caching, do I/O, and many other things that one may not normally expect from a library.

The statefulness is necessary for the bitcoin kernel's decidedly incremental approach to extracting our consensus engine. This approach favors:

1. Reusing existing code
...which allows us to be continually integrated with Bitcoin Core and benefit from our extensive test suite

2. Incremental decoupling instead of building from scratch
 ...which allows us to avoid having to prematurely optimize for a "perfect" boundary or API (tends to be highly subjective, non-obvious, may lead to unproductive bike-shedding before any meaningful work gets done)

If you are interested in a more high level motivational for the project and my approach to it, I wrote a blog post a few years ago: https://thecharlatan.ch/Kernel/.

`libbitcoinkernel` could also be used as an internal library for `libbitcoin_node`. The desired library organization is shown in [doc/design/libraries.md](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/doc/design/libraries.md). This is attempted in #28690.

## Areas with open work

### Developing an API for the library

Headers installed alongside the library should define a safe and stable interface for its users. Currently a C header provides support for validating scripts, transactions, headers, and blocks, as well as reading from the block store [bitcoinkernel.h](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/src/kernel/bitcoinkernel.h). This should be expanded over time to provide more features and flexibility to users.

The headers have bindings in:
* Python https://github.com/stickies-v/py-bitcoinkernel
* Rust https://github.com/sedited/rust-bitcoinkernel
* Go https://github.com/stringintech/go-bitcoinkernel
* Java https://github.com/yuvicc/bitcoinkernel-jdk
* C# / dotnet https://github.com/janb84/BitcoinKernel.NET
* Elixir: https://github.com/jurraca/ex_bitcoinkernel
* Javascript: https://github.com/musaHaruna/js-bitcoinkernel
* Swift: https://github.com/21-DOT-DEV/swift-bitcoinkernel

More bindings would be desirable for the following categories:
* Application developers and systems engineers (Kotlin, Dart, Zig, Haskell, Clojure etc.)
* Data analysis and research (R, Julia etc.)
* Data queries (e.g. PostgreSQL external data etc.)

Some work has also been done for expanding the current API, including:
* Script debugging: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35641
* Validating blocks without a chainstate: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35187

Ideas for more endpoints are gathered here: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/27587#issuecomment-4924935896

Some existing users of the library and its API are:
* Second's Ark implementation Bark: https://gitlab.com/ark-bitcoin/bark
* Floresta: https://github.com/getfloresta/Floresta
* A Rust full node: https://github.com/kernel-node/kernel-node
* A Swift iOS-compatible full node: https://github.com/Sjors/kernel-i-node

Another project is using the library with its own experiemental API: https://bitcoinbackbone.org/

### Error messages

The current API defined through the C header only has very rudimentary error handling. While it attempts to follow the philosophy that errors arising from unsanitized user input are programming errors, it does surface more concrete information on validation failures, as well as errors that arise from problems with the underlying system. These system errors are referred to as fatal errors. The current Bitcoin Core code does not always surface these fatal errors to the caller. Error handling is also baked into otherwise unrelated validity states. This should ideally be cleanly separated.

Fatal errors in particular are usually triggered by exceptions. However Bitcoin Core's exception handling is confusing and inconsistent. This should be improved by following C++ best practices around exception handling.

* Splitting error conditions from BlockValidationState: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35646
* Surface fatal errors as return types: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/29700

### Logging

It is also currently not possible to instantiate multiple kernel validation objects and distinguish between their log messages. The library currently only has a global logger. 

* A potential solution is #30342
* Improving the API to communicate that logging is indeed global: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34775

### Read-only kernel clients

The kernel library provides the functionality to read Bitcoin Core's data, like blocks, headers, and undo data, directly from disk without additional overhead. External applications like Esplora parse blk*.dat files directly for index building. This is problematic because Bitcoin Core's block storage is internal, changes sometimes (e.g. when introducing XOR-obfuscation), and provides no stability guarantees for external consumers. Reading this data through the kernel library can give these guarantees, as well as improve performance, since the block store might contain invalid blocks, or blocks from stale forks.

The current drawback to this approach is that leveldb, which stores the block tree and the chainstate, does not allow for readers in parallel processes. Bitcoin Core therefore has to shutdown before an external process using the kernel library can read its data. A pull request moving the block tree database from leveldb to a simple hand-rolled format, which would allow reading the data in parallel, was opened in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/32427.

A summary of how the kernel library might be used for reading data is provided [here](https://github.com/alexanderwiederin/bitcoinkernel-blockreader). Applications building on #32427 could validate this architecture as well as provide benchmarks for this approach over using Bitcoin Core's existing interfaces to read block data.

### Context-minimal validation

The current design of the library includes all the Bitcoin Core specific data storage methods. Alternative clients wishing to validate blocks therefore have to build the chain block-by-block and have to re-use the UTXO model.

However there exist projects and proposed alternative data models like utreexo, [swift sync](https://gist.github.com/RubenSomsen/a61a37d14182ccd78760e477c78133cd), [UHS](https://gnusha.org/pi/bitcoindev/CAApLimjfPKDxmiy_SHjuOKbfm6HumFPjc9EFKvw=3NwZO8JcmQ@mail.gmail.com/), and libbitcoin, that do not require a UTXO set for validation, but could still profit from re-using Bitcoin Core's Block validation code. [Floresta](https://github.com/vinteumorg/Floresta), a utreexo implementation, and a project working on swiftsync have voiced strong desire for these features.

There are a few possible directions to take here, including:
* Abstracting data readers and writers (e.g. an abstract block store: https://github.com/sedited/bitcoin/tree/blockstoreReaderWriter)
* Adding a function for validating blocks without the full UTXO set to the C header API: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35187
* Making validation functions require less context (e.g. stop passing the UTXO set to validation functions: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/32317)
* Reducing the `cs_main` lock scope (e.g. reducing locking during `AcceptBlock` https://github.com/sedited/bitcoin/tree/accept_block_reduce_lock)
* Exposing more validation functions, like `CheckBlock`, `AcceptBlock`, etc.
* Validation functions that only use the block tree, but don't persist chainstate and block data

Context-minimal validation might also be interesting for SPV clients, which wish to re-use only a subset of validation.

### `cs_main` split

Currently the `cs_main` recursive mutex protects not only the bulk of validation-specific mutable state, but also state in net processing. Ideally validation would have its own mutexes, that do not have to be shared with other functionality. Function calls requiring a lock to be held as a pre-condition to ensure consistent state transitions should be consolidated to allow internal locking. This could eventually allow users to process validation tasks and query for data in parallel with less locking contention. It also could allow parallel processing and better prioritization of network messages.

Some draft work towards this goal has been started
* Splitting the net processing mutex: https://github.com/sedited/bitcoin/tree/net_processing_lock_split
* Separate cuckoocache locks: https://github.com/sedited/bitcoin/tree/lock_cuckoocache
* Making CChain a copy-on-write data structure: https://github.com/alexanderwiederin/bitcoinkernel-proposals/blob/master/cchain-concurrency.md
* Replacing cuckoocache: https://purplekarrot.net/blog/bitcoin-validation-library-3.html

### Chainstate / ChainstateManager split

The Chainstate and ChainstateManager are currently tightly coupled, but need not be. In practice this means working with a single chainstate is often needlessly complicated. A draft split of the two classes has been attempted in https://github.com/sedited/bitcoin/tree/chainmansplit.

### Compile targets for embedded, web assembly, and proof systems

One step further than context-free validation would be a kernel API that can compile to architectures with reduced capabilities, e.g. no support for threading, file systems, or atomics. Adding these capabilities could allow the library to be used in embedded environments, e.g. as part of a validating lightning signer or SPV wallet. Targetting riscv bare metal, or llvm IR, could allow re-use in ZK proof systems as well as formal specification languages. As a first step, a basic RISCV bare metal CI job now ensures compatibility for these targets for the script evaluation code. This should be expanded over time to include more components. A long term deliverable of the project is to allow for zerosync style validation.

Eventually the goal here should be to provide a fully "sans IO" version of the API, akin to the original bitcoin consensus library.

### Evicting the mempool / plug-able policy

The mempool and its policy rules are currently inside the kernel library, but won't be exposed in the initial API version. Ideally the library should not force its users to re-use the existing Bitcoin Core opinionated implementation, but allow them to either define their own mempool or at least define their own policy rules. A rough proof of concept for removing the mempool from the library is implemented in https://github.com/sedited/bitcoin/tree/mempoolout.

The mempool is currently also the only dependent on boost within the library. Having boost as a dependency makes it a bit harder to build, and makes using the C++ headers in the library directly more annoying.

### Test vectors for the API

The project should provide test vectors to ensure language bindings around the header APIs are implemented consistently. 

* Bindings conformance tests: https://github.com/stringintech/kernel-bindings-tests

### Evicting AssumeUTXO  / AssumeValid

AssumeUTXO/Assumevalid are Bitcoin Core specific approaches to improving IBD speed. It is likely external users of Kernel will not want to be tightly coupled to Bitcoin Core specific processes, e.g., choosing the AssumeUTXO snapshots and assumevalid points. Philosophically, kernel should be as agnostic as possible and not tied to a particular implementation's decisions.

### Isolated kernel repository

Eventually Bitcoin Core could itself depend on a standalone kernel repository. Bitcoin Core would likely end up pulling in this project as a subtree. Some open questions around this subject are:

* How would the CI for this repository be set up?
* How would its own fuzzing and unit test setup look like?
* What does the release process look like?
* What is the governance of the project? E.g., is it under Bitcoin Core?

In many ways, this could be similar to how the libsecp256k1 is maintained in its own repository. Some steps towards this goal have been taken:
* Adding a dedicated internal kernel library that could be re-used directly by the project: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28690
* Removing the clientversion dependency from the kernel: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/32543
* Pruning unwanted headers from the library: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34079
* Remove translation.h usage from the kernel library: https://github.com/sedited/bitcoin/tree/kernel_rm_translation

### Idiomatic / ergonomic API types

The current API exposes a bunch of types that have side effects and are complicated to understand. For example, the relationship between `CChain` and `BlockMap` is difficult to communicate. Some of the primitive types hold cached information that is difficult to reason about, e.g. `CBlock`'s `fChecked` flag. Having the struct layout dictate serialization may also be surprising.While it is unclear what an ideal strategy for dealing with these is, there are a few avenues for chipping away at these difficulties, like introducing a separate CheckedBlock type, or tweaking the primitive types and their relationship.

* https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35569

---

## Action Items

1. If you have any questions, please post them below!
2. If you have any ideas for the future directions of the project, or want to work on one of the open areas, I'd love to talk about them and support you!
  
#### Other misc items that arose during review and should be tracked
* Cory's request for cleaning up the kernel interface functions of pointer and reference types: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/27636#discussion_r1202937682
* Marco's request for getting rid of exceptions in the `ArgsManager`: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/27491#discussion_r1189586654
* Russell's request for eliminating the BlockNotify signal: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/27636#discussion_r1193904693

Hi @sedited , I have been reviewing Kernel project issues and several pull requests to better understand the project so I can contribute meaningfully. Recently, I have been studying this outstanding [TODO](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/27636#discussion_r1202937682), and although I have thought about it, I am still struggling to fully reason about it. Below is my understanding and a naive approach I considered for implementing the TODO, which I suspect has some limitations.

### My understanding of the issue
Currently, the validation layer sends block-tip notifications using `const CBlockIndex&`. This is an internal Bitcoin Core structure that contains a large amount of chain state and metadata.

However, many consumers of this notification do not actually require the full `CBlockIndex`. For example, the UI layer ultimately converts it into a much smaller abstraction `BlockTip`.

The long-term concern is architectural as stated [here](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/27636#discussion_r1204902245https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/27636#discussion_r1204902245) we should avoid exposing internal Core structures across subsystem boundaries, especially in preparation for a future public kernel API. If `CBlockIndex` were exposed externally, then any internal changes to it could introduce API or ABI breakage for external users. This would tightly couple external code to Bitcoin Core internals.

To prevent this, a lightweight wrapper such as `BlockTip` would preferred, since it exposes only stable, minimal information.

### Current data flow
From what I understand, the flow currently works like this:

1. In `validation.cpp`, inside `Chainstate::ActivateBestChain()`, when a new best tip is connected, the code calls `m_chainman.GetNotifications().blockTip(..., *pindexNewTip, ...)`
2. This sends a `CBlockIndex` through the kernel notification layer.
3. In `KernelNotifications::blockTip()`, the node layer receives the `CBlockIndex` and forwards it to the UI system `uiInterface.NotifyBlockTip(state, index, verification_progress);`
4. Finally, the UI layer converts the internal `CBlockIndex` into a lightweight `interfaces::BlockTip` (`BlockTip{block.nHeight, block.GetBlockTime(), block.GetBlockHash()}`)
 

### My proposed change
My approach is to refactor the block-tip notification path so that `CBlockIndex` is no longer passed outside the validation layer.
Instead, when a block-tip notification is generated, the code immediately converts `CBlockIndex` into a lightweight `BlockTip` structure containing only: block height, block time, block hash. This simplified object is then passed through the rest of the system.

The complete code change can be found on my branch [here](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/compare/master...musaHaruna:bitcoin:refactor/remove-cblockindex-from-notifications)

### What I changed

- At the kernel boundary, I modified `kernel::Notifications::blockTip(...)` to use the `BlockTip` wrapper instead of `CBlockIndex`.
- In `validation.cpp`, I perform the conversion from `CBlockIndex`to `BlockTip` at the point where the notification is created.
- On the node and UI side, I reused `interfaces::BlockTip` and moved it to `src/interfaces/types.h`.
- I updated `uiInterface.NotifyBlockTip` so it now receives the simplified `BlockTip` directly instead of reconstructing it later.
- As a result, `handleNotifyBlockTip(...)` no longer needs to rebuild the tip data and can forward it directly.
- For `libbitcoinkernel`, I introduced a simple `btck_BlockTip` struct in `src/kernel/bitcoinkernel.h`, and updated the wrapper and example code accordingly.

### Core idea behind the change
The main idea is to convert `CBlockIndex` into a minimal representation once at the point of notification creation, and pass only the lightweight structure downstream.

This reduces coupling and prevents internal data structures from leaking across subsystem boundaries.

### Additional note
Regarding RPC impact: I am not fully certain how the change is expected to propagate there. In my branch, it did not require modifications in `src/rpc/*`. The only additional place I had to update outside the kernel and node notification flow was the `-blocknotify` hook in `src/init.cpp`, since it also listens to block-tip events.

Finally, I should mention that in my branch I did not strictly follow the conventional handle/view pattern, as I was mainly experimenting to understand the flow.

Recently, I have been studying this outstanding https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/27636#discussion_r1202937682, and although I have thought about it, I am still struggling to fully reason about it. Below is my understanding and a naive approach I considered for implementing the TODO, which I suspect has some limitations.

@musaHaruna Thank you for taking the time to go through this exercise, this is how I would have solved it too. I was never sure about authoring this change myself, because the same types are still being passed through the validation interface too. Removing them there seems a bit more involved, so I wasn't convinced that this would provide enough utility by itself to warrant the change. Your change is quite self-contained, and it would be nice to have at least one interface not push out internal types, but I'm not sure if it is worth it at this point in time.

We discussed that there should be a list of missing kernel functions, see this as a starter for discussions.

**Transaction acceptance checking** (broadly useful): 
mempool acceptance (`btck_chainstate_manager_process_transaction`), (wraps `ChainstateManager::ProcessTransaction`, i.e. mempool acceptance / policy validation), with a `btck_TxValidationState*` out-param like `btck_transaction_check`
package acceptance (`btck_chainstate_manager_process_package`) package/CPFP validation

**UTXO point lookup** (broadly useful): 
coin lookup by outpoint (`btck_chainstate_manager_get_coin`) returns `btck_Coin*` 

**Operational basics** (broadly useful): 
explicit flush (`btck_chainstate_manager_flush`), 
IBD predicate (`btck_chainstate_manager_is_initial_block_download`), 
verification progress (`btck_chainstate_manager_guess_verification_progress`), 
cache sizes (`btck_chainstate_manager_options_set_total_cache_size`), 
pruning (`btck_chainstate_manager_options_set_prune_target_bytes`, `btck_chainstate_manager_prune_up_to_height`)

**Chain surgery and recovery** (Possible interesting ? ): 
invalidate/reconsider block (`btck_chainstate_manager_invalidate_block`, `btck_chainstate_manager_reconsider_block`), 
integrity check (`btck_chainstate_manager_verify_db`)

**Chain event callbacks** (broadly useful): 
`btck_ValidationInterfaceUpdatedBlockTip`, `btck_ValidationInterfaceActiveTipChange`, `btck_ValidationInterfaceChainStateFlushed`

**Transaction-level accessors** (broadly useful): 
version/wtxid/weight/sizes (`btck_transaction_get_version`, `btck_transaction_get_wtxid`, `btck_transaction_get_weight`, `btck_transaction_get_virtual_size`, `btck_transaction_get_total_size`), 
scriptSig + witness (`btck_transaction_input_get_script_sig`, `btck_transaction_input_get_witness`), 
txid from bytes (`btck_txid_create`), 
merkle root (`btck_block_header_get_merkle_root`) needed for SPV-style merkle proof checking

**Chain metadata and parameters** (low prio): 
chain work (`btck_block_tree_entry_get_chain_work`), 
transaction count (`btck_block_tree_entry_count_transactions`), 
median-time-past (`btck_block_tree_entry_get_median_time_past`), 
consensus params (`btck_consensus_params_get_*`), genesis (`btck_chain_get_genesis`)

Below the fold stuff (low prio, if et al, see comment [below](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/27587#issuecomment-4927858674))

**Mempool event callbacks** (Possible interesting ? ): 
`btck_ValidationInterfaceTransactionAddedToMempool`, `btck_ValidationInterfaceTransactionRemovedFromMempool`, `btck_ValidationInterfaceMempoolTransactionsRemovedForBlock`; 

AssumeUTXO (`btck_chainstate_manager_activate_snapshot`), 

**Hosted mempool** (Possible interesting ?): 
options (`btck_mempool_options_create` + setters), 
query surface (`btck_chainstate_manager_get_mempool`, `btck_mempool_count`, `btck_mempool_contains`, `btck_mempool_get_entry_by_txid`, `btck_mempool_entry_get_*`)

Thanks for collecting those @janb84. I think we shouldn't be adding mempool and assumeutxo utilities any time soon. In my opinion clients should rather be thinking about how they can implement these features themselves and request the necessary functions and callback hooks from us. I am now linking to this list in the tracking issue.

I want to comment on "Compile targets for embedded, web assembly, and proof systems" section of the issue and propose some changes.

I'm trying to implement a RISC-V zkVM guest running a confidential version of proof-of-funds BIP-322 scheme.

The guest needs roughly this function:

```c
verify_script(tx_bytes, prevouts, input_index, flags) -> result_code
```

The function can't call OS, in particular it can't do IO and can't work with OS threads.

I propose these changes in the kernel library to enable this:

- a build mode that does not link pthreads or require OS thread support (a build option like `BITCOIN_SINGLE_THREADED`)
- a Script-verification-only kernel build target, so the resulting binary does not include chainstate, LevelDB, block storage, filesystem-dependent code, or unrelated kernel objects (`BITCOIN_KERNEL_SCRIPT_ONLY`)
- a way to build this target for constrained cross-compilation environments, such as RISC-V bare metal / zkVM targets (a set of CMake options)
  - For some targets this may also need caller-controlled allocation or a custom allocator hook.

The existing C header `bitcoinkernel.h` already exposes Script-related types and functions (e.g. `btck_script_pubkey_verify`). I propose to provide them as an small isolated sans-IO target.

I'm looking for feedback. I would like to implement this step-by-step, starting with `BITCOIN_SINGLE_THREADED` if that makes sense.

@starius If you haven't seen it yet, you might be interested in taking a look at this recently merged PR: #31425. You can now use `-DCMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME=Generic`, which allows you to bypass needing pthreads, atomics, boost headers etc.

Hi @sedited, I’ve been working on a few of the areas discussed in the tracking issue and would like to hear your thoughts.

I’ve been exploring the mempool separation under “Evicting the mempool / plug-able policy,” building on your [`mempoolout` proof of concept](https://github.com/sedited/bitcoin/tree/mempoolout). On [my branch](https://github.com/musaHaruna/bitcoin/pull/7), I’ve moved transaction and package admission into a dedicated node module and made the mempool interface’s locking and lifetime requirements explicit. I’ve also separated notification data from mempool entries. I considered opening a PR, but held off because I wanted to hear your thoughts first, particularly given the number of PRs already open.

I’ve also been working on separating block storage from chainstate management, following the pruning discussion in [#35627](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/35627). I put together [a prototype](https://github.com/musaHaruna/bitcoin/pull/3) and helped review [pzafonte’s implementation on his fork](https://github.com/pzafonte/bitcoin/pull/2). He has since opened PRs upstream based on that implementation, some in draft and others ready for review, and I plan to review those as well.

On the bindings side, I’d like to experiment with using the JavaScript bitcoinkernel bindings to handle part of [bcoin’s](https://github.com/bcoin-org/bcoin) validation. This is still an idea I want to investigate, but I think it could demonstrate the bindings in another full-node implementation and help identify gaps in the API.

I’ve also recently started looking at [#32427](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/32427) in connection with read-only storage. I don’t yet have the full context, but even while it’s in draft, I’d like to understand the PR better and see where I could help with review or testing. Any suggestions on what would be useful to look into would be welcome.

If there are areas you think need more attention, I’d appreciate any pointers on where my efforts could be most useful. Thanks!
